front: String matching problem — what is a 'valid shift' sft?
back: 0 ≤ sft ≤ n − m such that T[sft, …, sft + m − 1] = P, i.e. T[sft + j] = P[j] for all 0 ≤ j < m.

front: Naive String Matching — time complexity, and why?
back: O((n − m + 1)·m) — the outer loop tries all n − m + 1 shifts, and for each, the inner loop compares up to m characters. No information carries over between shifts.
Treat P and every length-m window of T as base-d numbers and compare the numeric fingerprints (O(1) comparison) instead of comparing strings character by character.

front: Rabin-Karp — how is t_sft+1 computed from t_sft in O(1)?
back: t_sft+1 = 10 · (t_sft − 10^(m−1) · T[sft]) + T[sft+m] — subtract the leading digit's contribution, shift up one digit, add the new trailing digit. The constant 10^(m−1) is precomputed once.

front: Rabin-Karp — why compute everything modulo a prime q?
back: Without it, p and t_sft can grow larger than a machine word for long patterns, breaking the O(1)-per-arithmetic-operation assumption. q is chosen so 10q still fits in a word.

front: Rabin-Karp — if t_sft ≡ p (mod q), is sft guaranteed to be a valid shift?
back: No — this can be a 'spurious hit' (false positive). An explicit character-by-character check is required to confirm. But t_sft ≢ p (mod q) DOES guarantee sft is invalid — no false negatives.

front: Rabin-Karp — expected vs. worst-case time complexity?
back: Expected O(n + m) with a well-chosen q (few spurious hits). Worst case degrades to O((n−m+1)·m), same as naive, if spurious hits are frequent.

front: FSM string matching — what does automaton state st mean?
back: The last st characters of T read so far equal P[0, …, st−1] (a prefix of P), and no larger overlap i > st holds.

front: FSM string matching — when is a match found, and what shift does it correspond to?
back: When the automaton reaches state st = m (the pattern length) while reading position sft of T. The valid shift is sft − m + 1.

front: FSM string matching — preprocessing and matching complexity?
back: Preprocessing (building the transition function δ): O(m·|Σ|). Matching pass over T: O(n) — a single left-to-right pass, no backtracking.

front: Can the FSM's overlap-length state decrease after reading a character?
back: Yes — δ(st, w) is redefined from scratch each step as the longest suffix of P[0..st−1]+w that is also a prefix of P, which can be shorter than st on a mismatch (unlike a naive counter that just resets to 0).

front: Does FSM string matching require the alphabet to be letters or digits specifically?
back: No — the FSM works over ANY finite alphabet (e.g. a course example uses Greek letters {β,δ,λ,σ}). Only the number of states (m+1) and the transition table size (m·|Σ|) depend on the alphabet, not the algorithm's correctness.
